name: Leo Tolstoy
role: Russian novelist and Christian pacifist and anarchist thinker (1828-1910)
summary: From the 1880s Tolstoy held that Christ's teaching forbids all violence and so rules out the state, the army, courts, prisons and taxes, which he saw as organised violence that enslaves workers. He condemned private property in land and rent, interest and wages, backed Henry George's land tax, rejected revolution and parliamentary reform alike, and called patriotism a fraud. He urged simple living, vegetarianism, chastity and a religion of love freed from Church dogma.

notes: Answers rest on his later writings (1886-1908), after his turn to non-resistance; his early views as a landowner and soldier are not used. Themes searched: government and state, war and patriotism, nation and empire, property, land and tax, money and wages, socialism and revolution, religion and church-state, sex and marriage, animals, technology, censorship, education and language. Not found in the texts reached: healthcare, minimum wage, trade, central banking, immigration, gender, race, LGBT and other modern policy questions, so those are null. Several answers (state functions, armed forces, police) come from his explicit rejection of violence and of the state, not from comments on the specific policy. I Cannot Be Silent was available only in part (the Wikisource transcription). The Britannica biography was blocked (403) and was not used; the Tolstoy-Gandhi correspondence on archive.org was not available.
